edits.old: If a secondary needs an entry that has rolled off its sync source's oplog, it cannot catch up using incremental replication; Alibaba says the member becomes too stale and enters RECOVERING. MongoDB's mongosync documentation says a transfer fails when unapplied source operations roll off, and its change-stream documentation says a resume token can fail after the associated event leaves the oplog. The window must cover the expected outage, lag, or migration copy interval. (high confidence)

evidence.quote: If a secondary node loses connection with the primary, it can only use [replication](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/replication.md#std-label-replication) to sync up again if the connection is restored within the oplog window.
If the required entry is missing, the node enters an abnormal RECOVERING state with a too stale to catch up error.
When operations that `mongosync` has not applied roll off the `oplog` on the source cluster, the sync fails and `mongosync` exits.
The oplog must have enough history to locate the operation associated with the token or the timestamp, if the timestamp is in the past.
then secondaries can stop copying entries from the oplog for up to 24 hours without becoming too stale to continue replicating.

edits.old: MongoDB defines the oplog window as the time between the oldest and newest oplog timestamps. Percona says that window depends on oplog size and write rate, and Netdata advises tracking the minimum window during peak write periods. A fixed byte limit therefore represents fewer hours as write volume rises; size from peak oplog generation and the longest lag or outage interval the deployment must survive. (high confidence)

evidence.quote: The oplog window is the time difference between the newest and the oldest timestamps in the `oplog`.
The length of the oplog window depends on the rate of Write operations in the system and the size of the oplog.
The actionable metric is timeDiffHours, and you must track its minimum value during peak traffic, not its average during quiet periods.
Size for peak write volume, not average. A bulk import, a backfill job, or a deployment that rebuilds an index can spike writes and temporarily compress the window.

edits.old: A minimum-retention setting is not a hard byte cap. MongoDB says mongod can grow the oplog beyond its configured maximum to preserve the retention period, which can exhaust disk under high write volume and long retention. Atlas also warns that high-volume bulk writes and migrations may fail to maintain the configured minimum window. Treat the configured retention as a target and check actual window and disk use during bursts. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23)
edits.new: A minimum-retention setting is not a hard byte cap. MongoDB says mongod can grow the oplog beyond its configured maximum to retain entries for the configured number of hours, which can exhaust disk under high write volume and long retention. Treat the configured retention as a target and check actual window and disk use during bursts. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/replSetResizeOplog.md
